verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, in keeping with the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus,
to Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
I am grateful to God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as my ancestors did, as I constantly remember you in my prayers night and day.
verse.note: In the Greek, “night and day” stands between the mention of Paul's prayers and the words “longing to see you” in the next verse, and it can go with either. The text attaches it to the prayers; the alternative is “night and day I long to see you.”

verse.text: Remembering your tears, I long to see you, so that I may be filled with joy.
I have been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, a faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and, I am convinced, lives in you too.
For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands.
For God did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but of power and love and self-discipline.
verse.note: The Greek does not distinguish capital from lowercase, and the word can mean either a disposition (“a spirit of cowardice”) or God's Spirit (“the Spirit God gave us is not one of cowardice”). Many interpreters think the Holy Spirit is in view, since verse 14 speaks of the Spirit living in believers. The lowercase rendering is used because it fits both halves of the sentence.

The traditional “spirit of fear” suggests fear in general, but this Greek word is not the ordinary word for fear. In the usage of the period it means cowardice, a failure of nerve regarded as a fault, and it leads directly to “do not be ashamed” in the next verse. Some modern versions have “timidity” and others already use “cowardice.”

This word occurs only here in the New Testament. It belongs to a word family for good sense and self-control, and can mean either the exercise of self-control or the act of bringing someone to their senses. “Self-discipline” and “self-control” are the usual modern renderings; the older “sound mind” takes it as a state of good judgment.

verse.text: So do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, or of me, his prisoner. Instead, share in suffering for the good news by the power of God.
verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: He saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace. This grace was given to us in Christ Jesus before long ages began,
verse.note: The Greek is literally “before age-long times,” using the plural of the word for a period of time with the adjective usually rendered “eternal.” The phrase points back before the whole span of history; translations vary between “before the world began,” “before the ages began,” and “before the beginning of time.” The same expression occurs in Titus 1:2.

verse.text: but has now been revealed through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the good news.
verse.note: This word was used in the Greek-speaking world for the visible manifestation of a god or the ceremonial arrival of a ruler, and “savior” was likewise a title given to gods and emperors. Elsewhere in these letters the word refers to Christ's future coming. Here it refers to his first coming.

verse.text: For this good news I was appointed a herald and apostle and teacher.
verse.note: The word names the official who made public announcements on behalf of a ruler or city, which fits the “good news” as a proclamation. “Preacher” now suggests someone giving sermons in church. Several modern translations also use “herald.”

Many manuscripts read “teacher of the Gentiles,” as in the King James Version. The shorter reading is found in a few early witnesses and is generally preferred by editors, on the view that the longer one was copied in from the parallel at 1 Timothy 2:7.

verse.text: For this reason I also suffer these things. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have trusted, and I am convinced that he is able to guard what I have deposited with him until that day.

note.term: what I have deposited with him
note.traditional: that which I have committed unto him

verse.note: The Greek is literally “my deposit,” a legal term for property left in someone's safekeeping. It can mean what Paul has entrusted to God (his life or his work) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the message), which is the sense the same word has in verse 14. The text follows the majority reading; the other has serious support.

verse.text: Hold to the pattern of sound words that you heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who lives in us.
You know this: everyone in Asia turned away from me, among them Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verse.note: Asia here is the Roman province of that name in the west of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. It is not the continent. Nothing further is known of Phygelus and Hermogenes.

verse.text: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain.
verse.note: Paul prays for the household of Onesiphorus here and greets it again at 4:19. For the man himself he asks mercy “on that day.” Some interpreters infer that Onesiphorus had died; others think he was simply away from home. The text does not settle it.

verse.text: Instead, when he came to Rome, he searched hard for me and found me—
may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day—and you know very well how much service he gave in Ephesus.
You then, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus,
and what you heard from me in the presence of many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be competent to teach others as well.

note.term: in the presence of many witnesses

verse.note: The Greek is literally “through many witnesses.” Most interpreters take this as “with many witnesses present,” perhaps recalling Timothy’s commissioning. It could also mean that the teaching reached Timothy by way of many witnesses who confirmed it.

verse.text: Take your share of hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No one serving as a soldier gets entangled in the affairs of everyday life, so as to please the one who enlisted him.
And if anyone competes as an athlete, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.
It is the hardworking farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops.
Think over what I am saying, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, according to my good news,
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for the public announcement of good news, including imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given here. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: for which I am suffering hardship, even to the point of chains, like a criminal. But the word of God is not chained.
For this reason I endure everything for the sake of the chosen, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory.
The saying is trustworthy: For if we died with him, we will also live with him;
verse.note: This is the same Greek adjective rendered “faithful” in verses 2 and 13. Said of a statement rather than a person, it means reliable, and “a faithful saying” is no longer natural English. The balanced lines that follow are widely thought to come from an early Christian hymn or confession.

verse.text: if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us;
if we are faithless, he remains faithful—he cannot deny himself.
verse.note: The verb can mean either “not believe” or “be unfaithful.” “Faithless” keeps the deliberate play on “faithful” in the same line and leaves both senses open. Interpreters also differ on whether Christ’s remaining faithful is a comfort (he keeps his promises despite human failure) or a warning (he is true to his word, including the denial just mentioned).

verse.text: Keep reminding people of these things, solemnly charging them before the Lord not to quarrel about words, which is of no use and only ruins those who listen.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided here between “before the Lord” and “before God.” The Greek text followed in this translation reads “the Lord”; several important witnesses and some modern editions read “God.” The sense is little affected.

verse.text: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker with nothing to be ashamed of, guiding the word of truth along a straight path.

note.term: guiding the word of truth along a straight path
note.traditional: rightly dividing the word of truth

verse.note: This rare verb appears in the Greek Old Testament (Proverbs 3:6; 11:5) for making a path straight. Its sense here is debated. Most modern versions give a general “rightly handling” or “correctly handling,” and the older “rightly dividing” presses the idea of cutting. The rendering here follows the Septuagint usage: the message is to be kept on a straight course, not diverted into the word-quarrels of verse 14.

verse.text: But keep clear of profane, empty talk, for those who engage in it will advance further into ungodliness,
and their message will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus,
who have strayed from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they are overturning the faith of some.

note.term: the resurrection has already taken place

verse.note: The teaching was probably that resurrection is a purely spiritual event already experienced by believers, for example in baptism or conversion, with no future bodily raising to come. The letter gives no further detail, so the exact form of the claim is uncertain.

verse.text: Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord turn away from wrongdoing.”

note.term: “The Lord knows those who are his,”

verse.note: Buildings often carried an inscription or seal marking ownership. The first inscription quotes Numbers 16:5 in the Greek version, from the story of Korah’s rebellion against Moses. The second echoes scriptural language (compare Numbers 16:26; Isaiah 26:13) but is not a direct quotation of any known passage.

verse.text: Now in a large house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor.
So if anyone cleanses themselves from these, that person will be a vessel for honor, made holy, useful to the master, prepared for every good work.
verse.note: “These” may refer to the vessels for dishonor, meaning the false teachers and their company, or more loosely to their teachings and conduct. The Greek leaves it open, and the translation does the same.

The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” a link that “sanctified” hides. It means to be brought into the sphere of what belongs to God. Most traditional versions use “sanctified,” while several modern ones use “made holy” or “set apart.”

verse.text: Flee the desires of youth, and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
But have nothing to do with foolish and ignorant debates, knowing that they breed quarrels.
And a slave of the Lord must not quarrel but be kind to everyone, able to teach, patient when wronged,
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, a person owned by a master, and fits the household image of verses 20–21. “Servant” is the traditional rendering and suggests a hired employee. In the Greek Old Testament “slave of the Lord” is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and David, which may color the phrase here.

verse.text: correcting opponents with gentleness, in the hope that God may grant them a turning back that leads to knowledge of the truth,
verse.note: “Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a humble, unassertive manner in dealing with others. “Gentleness” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

“Repentance” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets’ call to return to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repentance” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

verse.text: and that they may come to their senses and escape the devil’s snare, having been captured alive by him to do his will.

note.term: by him to do his will
note.traditional: taken captive by him at his will

verse.note: The Greek uses two different pronouns for “him” and “his,” and their referents are disputed. The majority view, followed here, is that both refer to the devil. Others read “captured by the devil, but freed to do God’s will,” or “captured alive by the Lord’s slave to do God’s will.”

verse.text: But understand this: in the last days hard times will set in.
For people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy,
verse.note: The Greek word covers insulting or defamatory speech against anyone, human or divine. In a list of social vices with no mention of God as the target, a first-century reader would most naturally hear abusive speech in general. Older versions have “blasphemers”; most modern translations have “abusive” or similar.

verse.text: heartless, implacable, slanderous, without self-control, savage, with no love for what is good,
treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,
holding to an outward form of godliness but having denied its power. Keep away from these people too.
For from among them come those who slip into households and take captive silly women who are heaped with sins and led by desires of every kind,
verse.note: The Greek is a diminutive of “woman” (literally “little women”) used contemptuously. It describes the particular women these teachers targeted, further defined by the phrases that follow, and is not a statement about women in general. Some translations render it “weak-willed” or “gullible women.”

verse.text: always learning and never able to come to a knowledge of the truth.
Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth—people corrupted in mind, who have failed the test as regards the faith.
verse.note: These names do not appear in the Old Testament. Jewish tradition gave them to the Egyptian magicians who imitated Moses’ signs before Pharaoh (Exodus 7–9), and the writer assumes the reader knows the story. Their “folly” in verse 9 refers to their eventual failure to match Moses.

verse.text: But they will not progress much further, for their folly will be obvious to everyone, just as the folly of those two came to be.
But you have closely followed my teaching, my way of life, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my endurance,
my persecutions, my sufferings—the things that happened to me in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra, the persecutions I bore. And out of them all the Lord rescued me.

note.term: in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra

verse.note: These are cities in the interior of Asia Minor (this Antioch is the one near Pisidia, not Syrian Antioch). Acts 13–14 recounts Paul being driven out of the first two and stoned at Lystra. According to Acts 16:1, Lystra was Timothy’s home region, so he would have known these events at close hand.

verse.text: Indeed, all who want to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted,
while evil people and charlatans will progress from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.
verse.note: The word originally meant a sorcerer or enchanter, and by this period it was commonly used for a swindler or fraud. Most translations take the general sense (“impostors”). After the comparison with Pharaoh’s magicians in verse 8, a hint of the older sense of “sorcerers” may be intended.

verse.text: But as for you, remain in what you learned and became convinced of, knowing the people from whom you learned it,

note.term: the people from whom you learned it
note.traditional: knowing of whom thou hast learned them

verse.note: The Greek text followed here has a plural “from whom,” pointing to several teachers—presumably Timothy’s mother and grandmother (1:5) as well as Paul. Many later manuscripts have the singular, which would refer to Paul alone.

verse.text: and that from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
All Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness,

note.term: All Scripture is God-breathed and useful
note.traditional: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable

verse.note: The Greek has no verb “is,” and the sentence can be construed in two ways: “All Scripture is God-breathed and useful,” or “Every God-breathed scripture is also useful.” The word for “all” can also mean “every,” pointing to each passage individually. Most translations and commentators take it as rendered here, but the alternative is grammatically possible and appears in the margins of several versions.

The Greek is a rare compound of “God” and “breathe,” found here for the first time in surviving literature. “Inspired” is the traditional rendering, but in modern English that word has weakened to mean little more than “brilliant” or “stirring.” “God-breathed” keeps the compound visible, and several modern translations render it this way or as “breathed out by God.”
Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous/just, righteousness/justice. Here the word refers to right conduct, the way of life Scripture trains a person in.

verse.text: so that the person who belongs to God may be complete, completely equipped for every good work.

note.term: the person who belongs to God

verse.note: The Greek noun is the general word for a human being, not the word for a male. “Man of God” is, however, an Old Testament title for prophets and leaders such as Moses and Elijah, and it is applied to Timothy in 1 Timothy 6:11. Many interpreters think the phrase here refers especially to the Christian teacher. Others take it of any believer, and the rendering leaves both open.

The Greek pairs an adjective and a participle from the same root, meaning “fit” or “complete” and “fitted out.” The repetition of “complete” in English reproduces that wordplay. The sense is of being fully capable for a task, not morally flawless.

verse.text: I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus, who is going to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom:

note.term: by his appearing and his kingdom
note.traditional: at his appearing and his kingdom

verse.note: In the best manuscripts “his appearing” and “his kingdom” are in the accusative case, the normal Greek way of naming what one swears by, so Paul is invoking them as witnesses to his charge. The older English rendering “at his appearing” follows later manuscripts with a different wording that ties the phrase to the judgment. “Appearing” was a word used for the manifestation of a god or the state arrival of a ruler.

verse.text: proclaim the word; be ready whether the time is right or not; correct, rebuke, encourage, with all patience and instruction.
For a time will come when people will not put up with sound teaching, but, following their own desires, will pile up teachers for themselves because their ears are itching,
and they will turn their ears away from the truth and wander off to myths.
But you, keep a clear head in everything, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, carry out your service in full.
verse.note: Most English versions have “ministry” here. The Greek word was an everyday term for service or a task carried out on someone’s behalf and did not name a religious office, whereas “ministry” now suggests a clergy profession. The same word is used of Mark’s usefulness in verse 11.

verse.text: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.

note.term: poured out as a drink offering
note.traditional: poured out as a drink offering

verse.note: In both Jewish and Greco-Roman worship, wine was poured out as an offering, often to complete a sacrifice; Paul pictures his approaching death this way. “Departure” was a common euphemism for death, and the word was also used of a ship casting off or soldiers breaking camp.

verse.text: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
verse.note: The image is from athletics and not from warfare: the noun is the ordinary word for a contest at the games, and the next clause continues with a footrace. “Kept the faith” may mean that Paul has guarded the faith entrusted to him or that he has stayed loyal to the end; the Greek allows both.

verse.text: From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.
verse.note: The crown is the victor’s wreath awarded at the games, continuing the athletic imagery of verse 7, not a king’s crown. The phrase may mean the crown that rewards a righteous life or the crown that consists in being declared righteous; interpreters are divided. “Righteousness” and “righteous judge” use the same Greek word-family, which also covers English “justice” and “just.”

verse.text: Do your best to come to me quickly,
for Demas has deserted me, because he loved the present age, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia.
verse.note: Many versions have “this present world.” The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, and it reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. Demas “loved” the present age, while verse 8 speaks of those who have “loved” the Lord’s appearing; the same verb is used in both places.

Some early manuscripts read “Gaul” in place of “Galatia.” Greek writers of the period also sometimes called Gaul “Galatia,” so even the reading translated here could refer to Gaul in the west and not to the region in Asia Minor. Most translations print “Galatia,” and the question remains open.

verse.text: Luke alone is with me. Pick up Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service,
and I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus.
When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus in Troas, and the scrolls, especially the parchments.
verse.note: The traditional “books” suggests bound volumes; the word at this period normally meant papyrus scrolls. “Parchments” is a Latin loanword for writing material made of animal skin, possibly parchment notebooks. What they contained is unknown, and some scholars take the word rendered “especially” to mean “that is,” making the scrolls and the parchments the same items.

verse.text: Alexander the metalworker did me a great deal of harm. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “coppersmith.” Although the word is formed from the term for copper or bronze, by this period it was used of smiths who worked in any metal, and some recent versions also have “metalworker.”

note.term: The Lord will repay him according to his deeds
note.traditional: the Lord reward him according to his works

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have a future tense, making this a statement of confidence; later manuscripts have a form expressing a wish, which lies behind the older English “the Lord reward him.” The wording echoes Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12.

verse.text: You too must be on your guard against him, for he strongly opposed our words.
At my first defense no one came to my side; everyone deserted me. May it not be counted against them!
verse.note: “Defense” is the technical term for a speech answering charges in court. Most scholars take this as the preliminary hearing of Paul’s current trial; an older view takes it as an earlier trial that ended in his release. The letter does not settle the matter.

verse.text: But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the proclamation might be carried out in full and all the Gentiles might hear it; and I was rescued from the lion’s mouth.
verse.note: The same Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples, so the phrase could also be rendered “all the nations.” “Gentiles” is chosen because Paul is describing his own commission as apostle to the non-Jewish world.

This is a biblical figure for deadly danger, echoing Psalm 22:21 and the story of Daniel. It has been taken to mean the emperor, Satan, or simply death; there is no agreement. It is probably not meant literally.

verse.text: The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Greet Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus.
Erastus stayed in Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus.
Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus greets you, and so do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers and sisters.
The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.
